lines: Sailors row a lifeboat built for 65 away, with only 28 aboard.
It is the first lifeboat lowered from the sinking Titanic.
Over 2,200 people are on the ship.
Her lifeboats can hold only 1,178.
Back in Belfast, Titanic could have carried 48 wooden lifeboats.
White Star chose sixteen wooden boats and four folding ones.
The law asked for even less. Sixteen boats, for 990 people.
So Titanic actually carried more than the rules required.
And the shortage was not about money or space.
You see, it's like an umbrella. It's for a quick dash to the door, not a whole day in the rain.
In those days, lifeboats were not meant to hold everyone.
They would ferry people to a rescue ship nearby.
That is exactly how it went when RMS Republic sank in 1909.
And White Star wanted a wide deck with open views of the sea.
A long row of lifeboats would have blocked them.
Then Titanic hits an iceberg in the dark.
She sinks in two hours and forty minutes.
Help is still hours away.
About 1,500 people die.
Titanic broke no rule. After her, inquiries led to new sea safety rules in 1914.

claims.claim: Lifeboat No. 7, the first lowered, left with an estimated 28 people despite a capacity of 65.
Over 2,200 people were on board; the lifeboats could accommodate 1,178.
Titanic, built in Belfast, could carry up to 48 wooden lifeboats, but White Star and Harland and Wolff chose 16 wooden lifeboats and four collapsibles.
Board of Trade rules required British vessels over 10,000 tonnes to carry only 16 lifeboats with a capacity of 990, so White Star provided more than legally required.
The shortage of lifeboats was not because of a lack of space nor because of cost.
Lifeboats were intended to ferry survivors to a rescuing ship, as in the 1909 sinking of RMS Republic where this played out flawlessly.
White Star wanted a wide promenade deck with uninterrupted views of the sea, which a continuous row of lifeboats would have obstructed.
Titanic struck an iceberg and sank two hours and forty minutes later with help hours away; around 1,500 people died.
Subsequent inquiries recommended sweeping changes to maritime regulations, leading to the International Convention for the Safety of Life at Sea in 1914.
